clinicalPearls: A focal dystonia producing involuntary, sustained or repetitive contractions of the masticatory, facial, and tongue muscles
Recognised patterns include jaw-closing, jaw-opening, jaw-deviating, and lingual dystonia, often triggered or worsened by speaking or chewing
Jaw-closing dystonia can cause bruxism, dental damage, and difficulty with mouth opening, while jaw-opening dystonia interferes with eating and speech
Many patients discover a sensory trick (geste antagoniste), such as touching the lips or chin, that transiently relieves the spasms
When combined with blepharospasm it constitutes Meige syndrome (cranial dystonia)
Secondary causes include dopamine-blocking drugs (tardive dystonia), neurodegenerative disease, and structural brain lesions, which should be excluded
Botulinum toxin injection into the overactive muscles is the principal treatment, supported by oral medication and dental appliances
reference.pathophysiology: Oromandibular dystonia is a focal dystonia affecting the jaw, mouth, and tongue muscles, arising from disordered motor control within the basal ganglia circuits and their connections, with abnormal inhibition and excessive co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles. This produces involuntary, patterned, often task-related movements of the masticatory and lower facial musculature. It may be idiopathic (primary) or secondary to dopamine-receptor-blocking drugs, neurodegenerative disorders, or structural lesions. The characteristic sensory trick, which temporarily reduces the dystonia through sensorimotor modulation, is a hallmark of dystonic disorders.
additionalDifferentials: Trismus from local or infective causes
additionalInvestigations: Detailed neurological examination for other dystonias and a sensory trick
Medication history to identify dopamine-blocking or other causative drugs
MRI of the brain to exclude a structural or degenerative cause in atypical or secondary cases
Surface or needle electromyography of the masticatory muscles in selected cases
Investigations for Wilson disease and other secondary causes in young patients
redFlags: Onset in a young patient suggesting Wilson disease or an inherited dystonia
Recent exposure to dopamine-blocking drugs indicating tardive dystonia
Additional neurological signs suggesting a neurodegenerative disorder
Acute severe jaw-closing spasm threatening the airway or causing tongue injury
reference.prognosis: Oromandibular dystonia is usually chronic; primary forms rarely remit but respond to repeated botulinum toxin injections combined with oral agents and appliances, allowing reasonable function. Secondary and drug-induced forms may improve if the underlying cause is addressed.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for temporomandibular joint dysfunction or simple bruxism
Failing to exclude Wilson disease in a young patient
Not recognising the sensory trick as a diagnostic clue
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
